title: Let It Cook: At Code with Claude, Developers Embrace AI That Codes, Tests, and Dreams
summary: The atmosphere at Code with Claude, Anthropic's two-day developer event in London, was one of eager acceptance. When engineer Jeremy Hadfield asked the packed room how many had shipped a pull request entirely written by Claude, nearly half the hands shot up. When he followed with, "Who here has shipped a pull request that was completely written by Claude where they did not read the code at all?" nervous laughter rippled through the crowd—but most hands stayed raised. It was a stark illustration of how rapidly AI coding tools have been normalized. Anthropic's message was clear: automation should be pushed as far as possible. Boris Cherny, head of Claude Code, explained that the default is no longer prompting Claude, but having Claude prompt itself. The AI now handles error messages, testing, and tweaking autonomously. "The key principle is getting out of Claude's way," said engineer Ravi Trivedi. "We like to say: 'Let it cook.'" A newly announced feature called "dreaming" takes this further. Claude Code agents now write notes to themselves, recording insights about specific tasks. When another agent works on the same codebase, it reads these notes to learn faster and avoid past mistakes. Over time, dreaming should help Claude improve its performance on a particular project. Yet outside the conference, skepticism is brewing. On forums like Hacker News, some developers argue that AI-generated code, shipped without proper human review, is creating a maintenance nightmare. "The only people I've heard saying that generated code is fine are those who don't read it," one user posted. When asked about these concerns, Anthropic's engineering lead Katelyn Lesse insisted that traditional best practices still apply. But she acknowledged the strain: some technical managers are exhausted trying to keep up with the volume of AI-produced code. Lesse compared Claude's current coding ability to a midlevel engineer—proficient at writing code but still needing expert oversight for system design and complex problems. The ultimate goal, product lead Angela Jiang confirmed, is for Claude to be able to build itself. As AI sprints ahead, the tension between productivity and prudence is only growing. The question isn't whether AI will write our code, but whether we'll still understand it.
why_it_matters: As AI begins to write more of the software that runs banking, medicine, and social media, the line between assistive tool and autonomous programmer is blurring. For a middle-schooler who may one day work in tech, this story is about more than coding speed—it's about whether we keep control over the digital world we build, or let machines build it faster than we can review.

background_read: AI-powered code assistants entered the mainstream with GitHub Copilot in 2021, which offered autocomplete-like suggestions inside the editor. Since then, tools like Anthropic’s Claude have progressed from simple line completions to agents that can write entire features, debug, and even manage testing.

Anthropic itself was founded in 2021 by former OpenAI employees with a focus on AI safety. Its coding product, Claude Code, is now used to generate pull requests that many developers ship without fully reading the code—a practice that would have been unthinkable just three years ago.

The London event highlighted the speed of this cultural shift. Historically, the dream of machines writing programs goes back to the early days of computing, but only recently has AI reached a level where it can function as a "midlevel engineer." Critics note that the pain of poorly reviewed auto-generated code often shows up later, when systems become hard to modify and understand.

The push toward 'dreaming' agents that keep notes and learn across tasks echoes longstanding ideas in artificial intelligence about learning from experience, but raises new questions: Who is responsible when something breaks, and will the next generation of coders still understand the systems that AI builds?

perspectives.description: Many developers feel AI coding tools free them from repetitive grunt work and let them focus on high-level design. Shipping features that once took days in hours, and letting the agent handle test errors, makes them feel more creative and less bogged down.

Critics argue that shipping unread AI-generated code is a ticking time bomb. Without human review, bugs and security flaws slip through, and future programmers may struggle to understand or fix a codebase that was written by a machine, leading to costly maintenance or even system failures.

Software engineering has repeatedly absorbed tools that were once feared: compilers replaced assembler, high-level languages replaced direct memory management, and IDEs replaced simple text editors. In this view, AI coding agents are just the next layer, and the industry will eventually develop new practices—like automated code audits—to keep quality high.

perspectives.perspective: The shifting role of the engineer
perspectives.description: If AI can write code at the level of a midlevel engineer, tomorrow's human developers may evolve into 'code architects' who define requirements, orchestrate multiple AI agents, and verify critical system logic, while the AI handles the low-level implementation. This shift could make software more accessible but also requires rethinking education and accountability.
